newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Onshore oil drilling in Nigeria makes Shell target.
newsitem.headline: Onshore oil drilling in Nigeria makes Shell target.

text.p: Producing oil from Nigerian creeks instead of from relatively inaccessible offshore platforms has exposed Royal Dutch Shell Group to attacks from impoverished local communities.
The latest crisis erupted when villagers seized oil flow stations on March 22 to protest against relocation of their local government council from the Ijaw area.
The last 52 of 127 Shell staff held hostage were freed on Thursday after delicate negotiations, but the incident showed how vulnerable the company's operations in Nigeria had become.
Unlike most oil firms in the troubled West African country, nearly all of Shell's installations are on land.
"Operating onshore leaves us more exposed than the others," said a senior Shell official, but he denied that the constant attacks had become intolerable.
"It's a challenging environment to work in but it is not an albatross, certainly not," he said.
Shell executives make clear the company is not about to abandon a profitable -- if hazardous -- operation.
"The question of a pullout does not arise," said one senior official.
Shell, which dominates business in Africa's leading oil-producing country, was forced to retreat in 1993 from the volatile Ogoniland in the southeast.

"Shell may not have anything to do with the local government changes but to many in the river areas where oil is produced, Shell is the only presence of officialdom," said Enock Fubara, a Lagos-based lawyer from the oil-producing Rivers State.
He added that Shell would be a target of people's frustration for as long as "the present unfairness" continued.

He was referring to a feeling in oil communities, made up of minor tribes in a country of 250 ethnic groups, that although Nigeria's oil wealth is derived from their own back yard they have no modern amenities to show for it.

To alleviate this, oil firms fund community projects in the oil-producing areas. Last year, out of a budget of $1.3 billion, Shell spent $36 million on community projects such as scholarships for local people, youth training, refurbishing hospitals and building schools.

"The communities that are beneficiaries appreciate the gesture, but the community projects are small compared to what is needed by the people," said Peter Pessu, an architect from Delta State, scene of the latest attack on Shell.
Shell says it spends more on community projects in Nigeria than anywhere else in the world, but submits that it could never become a substitute for local authorities.
"The unrest in the Niger delta is a symptom of frustration. They will not go away even if we spend $100 million annually," said a company executive. "We are just caught in the middle."
Operating on land exposes Shell staff, who live in neat, posh company quarters, to unemployed youth living in squalor.
"The temptation to pounce on Shell staff and to loot their property when an opportunity such as a riot situation arises is great," said Pessu.

People in the oil areas complain that Nigerian governments, always dominated by the major tribes of Hausa in the north, Yoruba in the west and Ibo in the east, use oil money to develop their areas and neglect the delta where the oil comes from.
This led to the Ogoni crisis when Nigerian author Ken Saro-Wiwa waged a campaign for self-determination for his 500,000-strong Ogoni tribe in the heart of the Niger delta.

Saro-Wiwa targeted Shell, which pumps half of Nigeria's two million barrels per day of crude oil output, demanding billions of dollars in compensation for Ogonis for ecological damage to their land from years of oil activities there.
But while his campaign won accolades from environmental pressure groups abroad, in Nigeria it was considered a threat to the country's economic lifeline.
Saro-Wiwa and eight minority activists were hanged in November 1995 over the murders of four Ogoni chiefs, provoking worldwide outrage.

"The international outcry that followed the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogonis in November had a serious impact on Shell's reputation globally," admitted Shell Nigeria's chief executive, Brian Anderson, in the company's annual review for that year.
